stories.headline: Pep Guardiola: Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo rivalry prolonged their careers
stories.summary: Pep Guardiola believes Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi would not have enjoyed such long and dominant careers without each other.
stories.body:
Pep Guardiola said he believes Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi would not have enjoyed such long and dominant careers without each other.

Ronaldo and Messi's rivalry dominated football for over a decade as they racked up a combined 13 Ballon d'Or awards and established themselves as the best two players of their generation.

They battled while representing Real Madrid and Barcelona (when Guardiola managed the Catalan club) respectively and featured at last summer's World Cup despite being in the twilight of their careers, before both retiring from international football.

"I think the two of them helped each other a great deal, if Messi hadn't had Cristiano, or if Cristiano hadn't had Messi, their careers would likely have been shorter," Guardiola told former Brazil forward Romario.

"But they had each other in their rearview mirrors, watching what the other was doing made them think: 'I want to be better than him, I want to win more than him.'"

Ronaldo, 41, retired from Portugal duty as the leading men's international goal scorer and appearance-maker after 146 goals in 234 games.

The 'Ballon d'Or of All-Time' winner, Ronaldo celebrated his 987th career goal when he scored for Al Nassr in Tuesday's AFC Champions League.

"Another competitive animal, someone who cares about nothing else than winning and proving himself," Guardiola said of Ronaldo.

"A goalscorer. With his right foot, his left foot, his head, he's extraordinary."

Guardiola never worked with Ronaldo but did coach Messi for four seasons at Barcelona.

He credits the Argentinian forward for much of his success while in charge of the Catalan giants.

- Cristiano Ronaldo goal tracker: Road to 1,000 career goals

- Columbus coach says Messi should've got red card in Miami loss: 'Everyone knows'

In a remarkable spell, Guardiola led Barça to 14 trophies, including two Champions Leagues and three La Liga titles.

Asked what enabled him to rack up so many titles as a coach, Guardiola said: "Messi! When you have such good players, you become good yourself. As a coach, you have to ensure that everyone follows the same path, understanding how they get along and which players can be paired together to make things work. But I've been with three incredible teams, all with incredible players, that's why we won."

After leaving Barça, Guardiola steered Bayern Munich to Bundesliga crowns in each of his three seasons at the club, including two domestic doubles, before enjoying a trophy-laden decade in charge of Manchester City, the club he left in the summer.

Asked if he tried to sign Messi after he departed Barcelona in 2012, Guardiola said: "No, I never reached out to him. I'm a Barça fan."

Guardiola said he is in awe of Messi, a record eight-time Ballon d'Or winner, who led Argentina to 2022 World Cup glory then, aged 39, helped the defending champions to the final last summer when they lost to Spain.

"I have never seen a player like him, someone with the ability to score three goals and provide three assists every three days," he said. "Very few are capable of such consistency, and he would do it in training, too, during small-sided games. In four years of coaching, I never saw him miss a single training session. He possessed this incredible competitive drive, that is what set him apart."

Guardiola likened Messi, now the captain of MLS side Inter Miami, to basketball legend Michael Jordan.

"When we all watched the Michael Jordan documentary, it struck me that a young Jordan was very much like Messi: someone who, alongside his teammates, was driven to be the absolute best," he said.

For Guardiola, there is no player that could ever reach Messi's level. He said: "No one, there are many good ones but I don't see anyone reaching that level; performing at such a high standard every three days for 15 to 20 years, and I don't think I ever will.

"There are records that people said would never be broken, yet they eventually are. [Former Jamaican sprinter] Usain Bolt's records will be broken one day, too, but to maintain that level of play for so many years, with that kind of plasticity... I just don't see it."

stories.headline: NHL Thanksgiving Panic Index: Which teams should be most worried?
stories.summary: Teams in playoff position on the holiday tend to stay there (77.1% since 2013-14). Who is in the best and worst shape?
stories.body:
At Thanksgiving, you either have a seat at the table or you don't. The same thing applies to Stanley Cup playoff berths: If teams don't have a seat at the table when the calendar flips to Turkey Day, the odds aren't in their favor.

Since the NHL switched the wild-card format in 2013-14, roughly 77% of the teams in playoff seeds at American Thanksgiving eventually appeared in the postseason. In 2025-26, 12 of the 16 teams in playoff positions made the cut.

There's still hope for those teams outside the bubble. Since the NHL expanded to 30-plus franchises, multiple teams every season made the playoffs while outside the picture at Thanksgiving. Over the past 10 seasons, 22 teams have rallied to make the playoffs after sitting outside the playoff picture at U.S. Thanksgiving.

There have even been six teams since 1995 that overcame deficits of seven points or more at Thanksgiving to make the playoffs -- the last one being the Edmonton Oilers in 2023, who were 10 points out.

So there's some hope, but there's also cause for concern -- and in some cases outright panic. Heck, even the teams in playoff seeds have their own anxieties.

Here is the American Thanksgiving NHL Panic Index, measuring the alarm for all 32 teams and organizing them into tiers. Let's start with the one team having a serene and blissful Thanksgiving in the standings.

Complete nirvana
Carolina Hurricanes

Imagine being the reigning Stanley Cup champions and then dominating the NHL after 24 games the following season, with basically the same groups of players. That is the Zen of the Carolina Hurricanes.

Their .813 points percentage (18-3-3) was tops in the league entering Wednesday night's games, with an NHL best plus-45 in goal differential. They appear poised for a potential repeat -- and you know GM Eric Tulsky and his front office aren't afraid to aggressively augment a roster that's already Cup-worthy.

Zero panic
Edmonton Oilers

Minnesota Wild

Vegas Golden Knights

The Wild led the NHL in points (41) entering Wednesday's games, while trailing only the Hurricanes in points percentage (.788) and goal differential (plus-37). Minnesota is 12-0-3 in their last 15 games (.900 points percentage!).

They have one of the league's most dominant offensive players in Kirill Kaprizov, whose 15-game point streak set a new franchise standard; one of the best goaltenders in Jesper Wallstedt, with a .924 save percentage and a 16-2-4 record; and one of the best defensemen in Quinn Hughes, who had 34 points in 24 games before the injury bug bit him. No, they don't have Dylan Larkin. But they have the assets they would have traded for Dylan Larkin, which means GM Bill Guerin will still go center shopping to complete his Cup-contending lineup.

After 26 regular-season games, Connor McDavid was projected to finish with 187 points. Adjusted for era, I'd say that's a gentlemen's 200 points. Regardless, Edmonton led the Pacific heading into American Thanksgiving, with over a dozen-point cushion over the fourth-place team. What's scary is that the Oilers are also a top-10 team defensively, thanks in part to Tristan Jarry and Devon Levi, who sorta-kinda-maybe could be the goalies that finally give Edmonton the stability they need in the crease.

Vegas nearly slipped to the next tier. The Golden Knights have their flaws -- less-than-elite team stats, a lack of scoring from their blue line, analytically fraught goaltending -- but they also have one incredible virtue: Playing in the Pacific Division. They were second to the Oilers and a country mile ahead of everyone else entering the American Thanksgiving cutoff.

Well, make that two virtues: Vegas has been uncharacteristically healthy for the most part this season. Even if that changes, please see virtue No. 1 for why that won't sink them. Stathletes projects Vegas with a 99.9% chance of making the playoffs.

Panicked but relatively pleased
Boston Bruins

Dallas Stars

Montreal Canadiens

New Jersey Devils

St. Louis Blues

Tampa Bay Lightning

All of these teams were in or right around playoff spots as the turkeys hit the tables in the U.S. In most cases, this was entirely predictable even before the season.

There's been more attention paid to disgruntled Lightning winger Nikita Kucherov's body language on the bench than to the fact that his team were a few percentage points from the Atlantic Division lead. Kucherov, Jake Guentzel and Brandon Hagel offensively and Andrei Vasilevskiy between the pipes are all key reasons why.

Just a shade behind the Lightning were the Canadiens, an Eastern Conference finalist last season. Before this week, the greatest development for the Habs was the arrival of Jacob Fowler as an NHL goaltending force and a rookie of the year favorite. But this week has all been about the arrival of Dylan Larkin, giving Montreal the elite center depth -- along with Nick Suzuki and Phillip Danault -- to contend with the league's elite teams in the postseason.

The Devils and Stars are a bit further back from their respective division leaders, but have to both be feeling pretty good about the first quarter of their seasons. New Jersey is buying newly acquired Connor Hellebuyck some time to find his game -- after missing the preseason and first month of the season -- with the fourth-best offense in the NHL, led by 30 points in 24 games for Jack Hughes.

The Stars are a mirror image of the Devils: They've had the goaltending all season in Jake Oettinger (plus-12.3 goals saved above expected, per Money Puck) but had the 25th-best offense through 23 games. The bottom line in both cases: These teams are finding ways to win.

The Bruins and Blues weren't playoff favorites in preseason prognostications, but here we are. Boston was in a playoff seed at Thanksgiving. The Blues are right on the bubble, having won four straight games.

The fascinating thing about Boston is its offensive balance. We all knew David Pastrnak was going to lead the team in points by a significant margin. But the Bruins had nine players through 23 games in double-digit points and saw Elias Lindholm -- a player who tapped out at 17 goals in each of the last two seasons -- match Pastrnak with 11 goals.

Meanwhile in St. Louis, Robert Thomas remains one of the NHL's most underappreciated offensive wagons, playing to a point-per-game pace while turning linemate Jimmy Snuggerud into a star, assisting on eight of his 14 goals.

Panicked until they're healthy again
Colorado Avalanche

Florida Panthers

New York Rangers

The Panthers are merely visiting this tier as they get two of their best players back from injury. Consider them "panicked but relatively pleased" after Wednesday.

Aleksander Barkov and Brad Marchand have both been cleared by team doctors to return to Florida's lineup. Both players have been limited to just two games this season. In Marchand's absence, his center Anton Lundell has found a spot between the Tkachuk brothers. Marchand is expected to skate with center Sam Bennett. We report this to give the rest of the league fair warning.

Cale Makar's return to the Avalanche couldn't have come at a more opportune time, as star center Nathan MacKinnon's injury recovery timeline was extended to 12 weeks. Colorado had a .630 points percentage through 23 games, which is a decent early-season cushion. Now their depth will be tested with Nate Dogg on the shelf for months.

The Rangers are here not because their current lineup faces any injury calamities. But all the success the Blueshirts have had -- which put them right around a playoff seed by Thanksgiving -- is undercut by the season-ending injury to star goalie Igor Shesterkin. Without him, there's a ceiling as to how good the Rangers are and could be this season. Wait 'til next year.

Panicked because their goaltending stinks
Anaheim Ducks

Utah Mammoth

Washington Capitals

Through 25 games, the Ducks had the league's worst team save percentage (.853). Last season, Lukas Dostal was their safety net. This season, he's playing like someone cut a hole in that net (minus-5.55 goals saved above expected via Stathletes). Ville Husso hasn't been much better. Anaheim simply doesn't have the team defensive prowess to sustain that kind of goaltending performance.

The Mammoth are giving up more goals (3.32 per game) than they're scoring (3.28) on average because of absolutely putrid goaltending. They rode Karel Vejmelka into the playoffs last season. His game has fallen apart this season, with an .872 save percentage and minus-5.8 goals saved above expected. Fans have clamored for Sebastian Cossa to rescue them. His analytics are generally just as bad; according to Stathletes, they're even worse (minus-7.8 goals saved above expected) than Vejmelka.

The Capitals could have qualified for several of these tiers in what's been a disastrous recent run of play and an overall bummer of a season. They can't find offensive cohesion, their blue line has been porous and Alex Ovechkin has scored as many goals as Igor Shesterkin this season during a not-all-that-fond farewell tour.

But in a rather stunning development, one of the league's best goalie tandems has been mediocre. Logan Thompson (.878 save percentage) and Charlie Lindgren (.849) are both in the negative analytically and have combined to give the Capitals the season-worst team save percentage in the league through 21 games.

Regression panicked
Nashville Predators

New York Islanders

Ottawa Senators

Seattle Kraken

Winnipeg Jets

PDO is a hockey metric that combines a team's shooting percentage and save percentage into a single number. It's considered a measure of "puck luck," while also acting as a predictor of sorts: Teams with an uncharacteristically high PDO are bound to regress to the mean, while those below average should swing upward at some point.

The Senators had the fifth-highest PDO in the NHL through 25 games, fueled by the third best 5-on-5 team save percentage thanks to Linus Ullmark. Their shooting percentage is above last season's levels as well.

The Kraken (sixth) and Islanders (seventh) are also riding the PDO train, with both shooting above their percentages from last season. The Kraken are in a more tenuous position, as they're underwater in several analytic categories (percentage of shot attempts, expected goals percentage among them).

The Jets were third in PDO over their last 10 games, going 8-1-1 in that span while shooting a preposterous 15.1% at 5-on-5. That'll obviously come back down to terra firma at some point.

The Predators are eighth in PDO over their last 10 games, but they face a more pressing question of sustainability: Can a team this top-heavy offensively compete for a playoff spot? Filip Forsberg, Steven Stamkos, Roman Josi and Ryan O'Reilly all have over 20 points; no other Predators skater had more than 10 heading into Wednesday.

Nihilistically panicked
Calgary Flames

Detroit Red Wings

Pittsburgh Penguins

Vancouver Canucks

All four of these teams are already tabulating their draft lottery odds, and that's probably fine.

The Flames and Canucks are in a rebuild. The Red Wings might as well be in one as they bid adieu to Dylan Larkin and bonjour to Michael Hage after their trade with Montreal.

The Penguins were a playoff teams last season and would have liked to be one again, but GM Kyle Dubas was a realist in his news conference last week, saying Pittsburgh would be focused on "future-oriented" moves. "We have to continue to make sure that this team isn't a decade-long in the abyss," he said. Sometimes, you lose to win.

Extremely panicked
Buffalo Sabres

Los Angeles Kings

Philadelphia Flyers

San Jose Sharks

The Kings brought on head coach Peter Laviolette to try to extend their playoff qualification streak to six seasons, but he can't even tease out a playoff push from this roster. Through 22 games, the Kings were third to last in the conference.

One of the reasons both MoneyPuck (43.8%) and Stathletes (70.3%) give Los Angeles decent playoff odds is because someone has to finish third in the Pacific Division. Stathletes gives the Sharks a 20.9% chance of making the postseason, but San Jose has yet to locate its swagger and stride after being a preseason glamour pick. We knew they'd struggle defensively. That they're 28th in goals per game is the real stunner.

But the Sharks are outscoring the Flyers so far this season. Last spring, Philly made the playoffs and won a round. Five months later, fans are flying airplanes with banners calling for coach Rick Tocchet to be fired, while team executives are flying across Canada to make sure Matvei Michkov doesn't want to be traded.

The Sabres broke the longest playoff drought in NHL history last season, lost a couple of key players and are now trying to claw their way back into the wild-card race. Stathletes gives them a 20.6% chance of making the playoffs, which means there's around an 80% chance all the good vibes from last season get swallowed up like a small car in a Western New York blizzard.

Beyond panicked
Chicago Blackhawks

Columbus Blue Jackets

Toronto Maple Leafs

The Blackhawks were supposed to crawl out of the primordial ooze of their rebuild this season. Injuries to Connor Bedard and Bowen Byram, combined with not being a good hockey team at all, scuttled those hopes.

The Blue Jackets nearly made the playoffs last season, but the vibes have been horrible every moment after that. Norris winner Zach Werenski expressed doubt about his future with the team. Winger Kirill Marchenko was traded upon request. Stathletes gives Columbus a 1.2% chance of making the playoffs. That's bad!

Yet not as bad as the team to whom they traded Marchenko, the Maple Leafs, who had a 0.2% chance of making the playoffs heading into Wednesday night. The Leafs could have been in the "panicked because their goaltending stinks" tier, seeing as how Sergei Bobrovsky's atrocious season (minus-6.98 goals saved above expected) has cost Toronto dearly. But the Leafs have problems that extend well beyond the crease. Coach Jim Hiller was hired by new GM John Chayka. He might not make it through this season.

Now that's a panic move.

PUCK HEADLINES
DATELINE: Michigan
I didn't appreciate the people who wanted to pour salt in the Red Wings' wound over the Larkin trade by suggesting University of Michigan center Michael Hage -- the centerpiece of that trade return from Montreal -- might opt never to sign a contract with his new rightsholder. Furthermore, there were people entertaining the idea that Hage would become an NCAA free agent ... and eventually sign with Montreal. That's just cruel.

It was also nonsensical. Detroit interim GM Shawn Horcoff had to have some understanding with Hage prior to making the trade with Montreal, or else he's not making that trade. Like, perhaps, from his son Will Horcoff, who is Hage's housemate and teammate at Michigan?

Hage himself ended the drama in an interview with Nick Cotsonika of NHL.com, saying he plans to sign with the Red Wings after Michigan's season is over. "After, hopefully, we win a national championship," he said.

And hopefully that puts the speculation to bed.

DATELINE: PITTSBURGH
When Penguins GM Kyle Dubas spoke with the media last week, the topic of Sidney Crosby's future naturally came up. The captain is 39. He's scored 15 points in 23 games for a Penguins team near the bottom of the Eastern Conference. He's averaging under 20 minutes per game for the second straight season.

Most crucially, he's an unrestricted free agent next summer, on a team that's going to trade away a handful of veterans for "future-oriented" assets.

"I think in Sid's case, he's as unique as it gets," Dubas said. "We want to get into this as far as we can, have an indication about where we're at and where we're going, and make sure everyone's comfortable with that. He's owed all the respect in the world. If he wants to be here, that's great, and that's obviously what we would love as well."

But Dubas also stressed that Crosby, Evgeni Malkin and Kris Letang are "at an age where it's not just a given they're going to keep playing. We all wish them to play forever but, at some point, the time comes."

Crosby's agent Pat Brisson told Sportsnet's "Real Kyper and Bourne" show on Monday that Sid's goal is only play for the Penguins.

"Kyle came out last week and said he's going to trade for futures. He has a responsibility right now to move these parts that he's going to move," Brisson said. "Sid is evaluating and watching. His goal is to be a Penguin forever. That's always been his goal. That's why he's in no rush."

When people talk about Crosby leaving a losing team to play for a Cup contender, the thing they miss is that the losing team is the Pittsburgh Penguins. The team that drafted Crosby, where he won three Stanley Cups, where he's comfortable and where he's never wavered in wanting to play his entire career.

Again, he's 39. The writing has been on the wall in Pittsburgh for quite some time, having not won a playoff series since 2018. I've long believed -- maybe hoped -- Crosby would end up on a contender for one last championship push before his Mount Puckmore-worthy career ends.

But I'm starting to believe that, like Brisson said, Crosby will be a Penguin forever. I've come around to the idea he wants to end his run with the same organization with whom he began it. Maybe he's won enough where mentorship will be as rewarding as another playoff run. Maybe he wants to act as the bridge between eras in Pittsburgh.

Or, and please understand I hope this isn't the case: Maybe we're watching the farewell tour now and don't even realize it. As Dubas said: "At some point, the time comes."

stories.headline: Man City told regulator 'has the stomach' to challenge owners after charges
stories.summary: The chair of the Independent Football Regulator says his organisation "has the stomach" to take on Manchester City's owners should it need to.
stories.body:
The chair of the Independent Football Regulator says his organisation "has the stomach" to take on Manchester City's owners should it need to.

The IFR has the power to force directors off boards and even to force owners to divest from clubs in the most serious cases where they are found to be unsuitable.

City have been found guilty of breaching Premier League rules over a nine-season period by an independent commission. The verdict, published in September, found they clearly intended to circumvent league rules through a series of "sham" arrangements which inflated revenues and disguised losses.

City have appealed against the verdict, but should it be upheld it seems almost certain the IFR would then conduct its own assessment, and Kogan was adamant there would be no fear from his organisation in doing so, despite the size of the club and the political connections of its owner Sheikh Mansour, who is the deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.

"We will absolutely have the stomach [to take on City]," he told MPs on the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport select committee.

"Would I, given my choice with an organisation that has a relatively new, fairly young staff that's been going for less than a year, would I have chosen to have this particular issue in our laps this early? Well, probably not.

"But the truth is, if we don't act, assuming those circumstances are triggered, if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?

"We have to absolutely clearly be seen to be doing the job that you, as legislators, have asked us to do, and we absolutely will do that, whatever that means.

"Forget the name of the club. Forget the size of the club. Forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size.

"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League, and by any judgment that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.

"Does the evidence, if we come to assess it in relation to individuals, stand up in terms of the legislation as being a cause for concern? And if it is, we will have to act appropriately. And that is the only test, not the politics around it, not the place where it came from, not the size of the club. It is the only test because without that, you cannot have an effective regulator."

MPs questioned how any legal action against City could be funded.

IFR chief executive Richard Monks told MPs it had been given "assurances" that the Government would provide cash to take on any litigation arising from any major case, which he stressed would only be embarked on if the advice was that the regulator would win.

In that instance, he said, the Government would be paid back directly. If the case was lost, the clubs would return the money to the Government through the levy they pay to run the IFR.

- Kevin De Bruyne: Man City achievements will not be tainted if appeal fails

- What's next for Man City? Appeals, possible punishments, how long it could take

- How a mass Man City player exodus would warp the transfer market

Monks said where forcing an owner to divest is considered appropriate, a sale can be forced even if the owner does not feel the sale price reflects a club's value.

"If we determine that an owner is unsuitable, then the owner has a period of time in which to then sell the club on their own behalf," he said.

"That is not set down in the [Football Governance] Act. That could be three months. That could be six months. Then, if they are unable or unwilling to sell in that time, then we appoint a third party who will oversee that sale, and the third party will get the best possible price for that club within a set time period.

"If that price is under what the owner is prepared to sell [for], so be it."

stories.headline: NBA reveals $11B arena initiative to boost efforts for Europe league
stories.summary: The long-planned NBA-backed league in Europe took another step toward becoming reality with the unveiling of a plan that targets nearly $11 billion in funding for the development and renovation of arenas around the continent.
stories.body:
The long-planned NBA-backed league in Europe took another step toward becoming reality Wednesday with the unveiling of a plan that targets at least 10 billion euros (nearly $11 billion) in funding for the development and renovation of arenas around the continent.

The NBA said a group of global investment firms -- including Apollo Sports Capital, Ares Management, Arctos, Blackstone, HPS Investment Partners, J.P. Morgan, Sixth Street and Stonepeak -- are supporting the initiative. It will, the league said, provide "prospective clubs and ownership groups with access to sustainable capital and the NBA's expertise to develop modern arena facilities and, where appropriate, surrounding districts."

The NBA and FIBA, which are partnering to launch the European league, have said it will begin play next fall.

"We've seen firsthand how state-of-the-art arenas and the related developments around them can transform basketball teams and their surrounding communities," NBA commissioner Adam Silver said. "As we prepare to launch a new league in Europe alongside FIBA, we see a significant opportunity to help clubs develop facilities which both build on the unique traditions that define European basketball while also elevating the fan experience and attracting many more live events."

The investors will partner with "participating clubs, ownership groups, local developers and other service providers to develop world-class arenas" that would become year-round destinations, the NBA said.

In a collective statement, the investors said they would help honor "the passion and traditions of European basketball fans and supporting lasting economic growth in the communities where the game means so much."

The NBA and FIBA have taken on the Europe project in large part because they believe the potential -- both from a commercial standpoint and a competitive one -- is not close to being realized. A new league has been talked about for years, with a plan to move forward getting announced in March 2025. Many of the NBA's top players of this era, including San Antonio's Victor Wembanyama (France), Miami's Giannis Antetokounmpo (Greece), the Lakers' Luka Doncic (Slovenia) and Denver's Nikola Jokic (Serbia), hail from Europe.

The NBA has long maintained that world-class arenas can drive immense growth -- thousands of jobs, millions of tickets, billions in economic impact -- not just for basketball franchises but also for the cities where they are located as centers of economic and cultural activities. Those arenas aren't easy to find in Europe, at least compared to more state-of-the-art venues in the U.S.

Current target countries for the NBA-FIBA endeavor are known to include Britain (potential host cities of London and Manchester), France (Paris and Lyon), Spain (Madrid and Barcelona), Italy (Rome and Milan), Germany (Munich and Berlin), Greece (Athens) and Turkey (Istanbul). None of those cities have been formally announced as NBA Europe selections.

stories.headline: WNBA players elect Elizabeth Williams as union president
stories.summary: Sky center Elizabeth Williams was elected president of the Women's National Basketball Players Association and will replace Nneka Ogwumike, who had been in the role since 2016.
stories.body:
Chicago Sky center Elizabeth Williams was elected president of the Women's National Basketball Players Association and will replace Nneka Ogwumike, who retired after being in the role since 2016.

Williams, who will serve out the final two years of Ogwumike's term that began earlier this year, was picked by players on Tuesday over Breanna Stewart of the New York Liberty and Gabby Williams of the Golden State Valkyries, a source with knowledge of the ballot told ESPN.

A 12-year veteran, Williams joined the WNBPA executive committee in 2018 and served four two-year terms. She has been at the bargaining table for two CBAs, including the most recent agreement that raised maximum player salaries to over $1 million.

"One of my main goals as president is to increase the engagement of the younger members of this union," Williams said in a statement to WNBPA player representatives. "I know the value of diverse voices in these conversations. We may not always agree, but I want to make sure every player knows that her voice is being heard.

"This is the strength of our union. I am grateful for what we have accomplished over these last few years, and I'm excited about the potential for a new opportunity to serve."

The WNBA will also have a new face leading the league office as commissioner Cathy Engelbert is retiring at the end of the year. A search for her replacement is ongoing.

Williams will lead the executive committee comprised of Napheesa Collier (1st vice president), Veronica Burton (secretary), Chelsea Gray (treasurer), and three additional vice presidents: Alysha Clark, Ezi Magbegor, and Maya Caldwell.

Burton, Gray, Magbegor and Caldwell join the executive committee for the first time.

"These election results reflect the strength of our union and the power of player leadership," WNBPA executive director Terri Carmichael Jackson said in a statement. "Congratulations to Elizabeth and each of our newly elected and returning Executive Committee members, whose collective experience, diverse perspectives, and commitment will help guide the WNBPA into its next chapter.

"As we turn our focus to implementing our transformational CBA and building on the progress our members have fought so hard to achieve, our greatest strength remains our unity, our democratic process, and our unwavering commitment to one another."

Williams, who was selected fourth overall in the 2015 WNBA draft out of Duke and was the 2016 Most Improved Player, becomes president after a lengthy period of stability in union leadership.

Ogwumike, the outgoing WNBPA president, announced her WNBA retirement during the 2026 season. An 11-time All-Star and the 2016 MVP, Ogwumike has served as WNBPA president since 2016, presiding over two collective bargaining agreement negotiations and shaping the social justice activism that defined the player body during her tenure.

stories.headline: Heeney headlines returning Swans at pre-season training
stories.summary: After months of off-field turmoil in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal, the Sydney Swans have welcomed back four AFL players for pre-season training.
stories.body:
The Sydney Swans have welcomed back their embattled AFL quartet to training after months of off-field turmoil following the Pullman Hotel scandal.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice signalled their intent to resurrect their playing careers by taking part in the club's first-to-fourth-year pre-season training on Monday.

High-profile forward Tom Papley was also in attendance at Sydney's Bat and Ball Oval after being slapped with a three-game ban by the AFL for a positive roadside drug test.

Monday's session marked the first time Heeney, Warner, Bice and Jordon have officially trained with the Swans since serving a season-ending suspension for what the club termed a "serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

That AFL-endorsed suspension was also served by now-North Melbourne player Nick Blakey.

Separate from the bans, Heeney, Warner, Jordon and Blakey were under investigation after three women made reports of sexual assault to Victoria Police.

Police have since confirmed the players would not be charged due to insufficient evidence.

Civil claims are still being prepared against relevant parties.

Monday's session was a relaxed affair, with the club also welcoming draftees Caylen Murray, Mason McGroder, Mitchell Knevitt and Brady Wright.

Players undertook the usual pre-season conditioning programs, doing running drills before moving on to contest work and a short match simulation.

It wasn't the first time Heeney, Warner, Jordon and Rice had trained with teammates, having done informal sessions at Centennial Park.

Papley, one of the team's most experienced players, returned to training as he prepares to face Waverley Local Court for driving with a suspended licence on November 26.

The 30-year-old was pulled over by NSW Police for a random roadside drug test on November 2, with checks revealing his licence was suspended due to non-payment of a parking fine.

The initial roadside test returned a positive reading, and a secondary sample of oral fluid was taken.

That secondary sample returned a positive roadside test for the presence of cocaine and MDMA.

On top of his AFL ban for conduct unbecoming, Papley was fined $722 by police and his licence will be suspended for three months.

Papley spent most of Monday's training session with the rehabilitation group alongside fellow forwards Logan McDonald and Hayden McLean after undergoing surgery on both knees.

He suffered a grade-two medial collateral ligament strain in his right knee in the club's preliminary final loss to Fremantle, before undergoing an arthroscopy on his left knee to address a historic issue.

Papley will miss all pre-season matches and the club's opening rounds against Geelong, Essendon and GWS.

stories.headline: 'Little disappointing': Munster makes call on Storm offer
stories.summary: Melbourne's fight to keep Cameron Munster and Harry Grant has been made harder after the former rejected the club's latest offer.
stories.body:
Cameron Munster has declared all options are on the table after officially rejecting a deal to stay in Melbourne and labelling the Storm's latest offer as "disappointing".

With Melbourne already facing a battle to retain Harry Grant, the Storm are now officially fighting a retention war on two fronts after Munster's call.

The Melbourne superstar admitted on Tuesday that Grant's future could play a role in his own call, as well as Craig Bellamy's impending retirement at the end of 2027.

As it stands Munster will not take up an offer from the Storm that is understood to have been for one year with an option for a second.

"I have declined it," the Queensland State of Origin captain said at a Maroons sponsor announcement with Westpac.

"I am not saying I am going to leave Melbourne. Just with the terms and conditions that they put out to me, it is probably something that is a little disappointing.

"But it's a business, I am not stupid."

Munster admitted his own form had not been good enough for the Storm last season as they missed the finals for the first time in his career.

And in turn, the 32-year-old conceded the offer may have been as a result of that.

"That (offer) just makes my job a little bit harder. But it's also a bit of a challenge saying I am not where I need to be," he said.

"Maybe I need to be a little bit better to earn that contract that we're looking from.

"And maybe it is a little bit of a kick up the bum from them. I am not too sure where we'll go from here but all options are open at the moment."

Munster's rejection comes after Grant met with Gold Coast officials last Friday and officially received an offer to join the Titans.

It is understood Melbourne's offer for the Queensland dummy-half will either be worth similar or more than the Titans.

But Gold Coast are hopeful of luring the hooker north, given his relationship with ex-Maroons assistant coach Josh Hannay and prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui.

The Titans officially released AJ Brimson to the PNG Chiefs on Tuesday on a three-year deal, with the money from the centre used to help pursue Grant.

NSW prop Stefano Utoikamanu is also off contract at Melbourne at the end of next year and has also been linked to the Sydney Roosters.

At the same time Bellamy's retirement at the end of next season is proving a challenge for the Storm, given he is like a father figure to Munster.

"When you look at someone like Craig as a coach, he is a great coach and I have so much respect and have admired him for such a long time," Munster said.

"It's going to be different at the club. I'm not too sure where the club wants to go with all that stuff.

"I don't know who they are going to get and I'm sure it will be a daunting job coming after him."

Munster also confirmed he will likely follow the Cameron Smith route and give away representative football at some point to focus on club duties.

"It definitely has (crossed my mind)," Munster said.

"The hard thing for me is giving up the captaincy.

"Once I start declining (I will look at it) and I thought I was declining. But after my last few games for the World Cup I am pretty confident I can get back to that."
